cases.question: What are the two golden rules for a safe and productive laboratory?
cases.answer:
1) Whenever you use a lab, it is your responsibility to see that unsafe conditions are corrected immediately; and [Page 2]
2) Always leave a laboratory in better condition than when you found it. If we all take on this level of personal responsibility, our facilities can only improve. [Page 2]

cases.question: What is the purpose of this safety manual, and who ultimately owns experiment safety?
cases.answer: The purpose of the manual is to make all users of IIT Hyderabad Mechanical & Aerospace Laboratory facilities aware of safety and emergency protocols (do’s and don’ts) that must be followed [Page 5]. The ultimate responsibility for conducting a safe experiment resides with the experimentalist [Page 5].

cases.question: List the five essential laboratory safety principles in section 1.1.
cases.answer:
* Following rules [Page 5]
* Personal responsibility towards safety [Page 5]
* Trust system more than people [Page 5]
* Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) [Page 5]
* Prompt response to non-conformity, incidents and emergencies [Page 5]

cases.question: Why can laboratory staff not be treated as the sole safeguard for every operation?
cases.answer: The staff cannot oversee or supervise operations all the time [Page 6]. Under these conditions, any inconsiderate user can endanger their own and the safety of others [Page 6]. Most problems, incidents, and violations in the laboratory result from haste [Page 6].

cases.question: What does HIRA require laboratories to do with workplace risks?
cases.answer: HIRA requires identifying, quantifying, and assessing the potential risk in the workplace [Page 6]. Risk control through elimination, substitution, reduction, engineering control, and administrative control is essential for a safer work environment [Page 6]. Risk assessment must be carried out qualitatively and quantitatively [Page 6].

cases.question: Who is the first contact for a departmental lab safety concern, and where is an unresolved issue escalated?
cases.answer: The Department Safety Champion or Safety Coordinator is the primary contact point for any safety-related issue or concern in a departmental laboratory [Page 7]. If the champion or coordinator cannot resolve the issue, it needs to be put before the safety committee through office@mae.ith.ac.in [Page 7].

cases.question: How does section 2.1 define a hazard?
cases.answer: A hazard is a substance, object, or situation that may result in an accident (injury or damage) [Page 8].

cases.question: What formula is used for qualitative risk assessment?
cases.answer: The formula for qualitative risk assessment is Risk = Severity x Likelihood [Page 10]. This involves making a formal judgment on the consequences and probability [Page 6].

cases.question: Name the effects of accidents listed in the manual.
cases.answer:
● Injury to Person [Page 8]
● Equipment Damage [Page 8]
● Material Loss [Page 8]
● Financial Loss [Page 8]
● Loss of Business [Page 8]

cases.question: Give four examples of mechanical hazards from section 2.3.1.
cases.answer: Four examples of mechanical hazards from section 2.3 are: Blades, Moving or rotating belts or chains, Gears, and Shafts [Page 9].

cases.question: In Table 1.1, what risk score results from Almost Certain likelihood and Catastrophic consequence?
cases.answer: Almost certain × Catastrophic: 25 [Page 10]

cases.question: Using Table 1.1, what is the assessed risk for Possible likelihood and Moderate consequence?
cases.answer: Possible × Moderate: 9 [Page 10]

cases.question: According to Table 1.2, what does severity level 4 mean?
cases.answer: Severity level 4: Major Serious injury (injuries) requiring special Medical Treatment and/or Hospitalization [Page 11]

cases.question: In Table 1.3, which probability category is D and how is it described?
cases.answer: The probability category D is described as Unlikely [Page 10].

cases.answer: -Consider alternatives to doing the Extreme would be likely that a activity. permanent, debilitating injury - Significant control measures will or death would result need to be implemented to ensure safety - Immediate action required by [Page 12]

cases.question: In Table 1.6, what does elimination mean?
cases.answer: Elimination means to remove the hazard completely from the workplace or activity [Page 13].

cases.question: What two engineering-control examples are given in Table 1.6?
cases.answer:
The two engineering-control examples given are:
*   Redesigning a machine or work process to make it safer, such as raising a bench to reduce bending [Page 13].
*   Isolation, which involves separating people from the hazard, like a safety barrier [Page 13].

cases.question: When should PPE be considered as a risk-control method?
cases.answer: PPE should only be considered when all other control methods are used [Page 14]. Examples of PPE include eyes (safety glasses), face (face shield), head (hard hat), ear (ear plugs), hand (rubber gloves), foot (safety shoes), body (rubber apron), and respiratory (respirator) [Page 14].

cases.question: Whose prior approval is needed before using restricted chemicals or materials?
cases.answer: Prior approval from the PI or laboratory supervisor is needed before using restricted chemicals and other materials [Page 14]. This is also required for using highly hazardous materials or conducting certain higher-risk experimental procedures [Page 14].

cases.question: Is food or drink allowed inside Mechanical and Aerospace laboratories?
cases.answer: No, food or drink should never be allowed inside the lab [Page 15]. Refrigerators storing hazardous materials must have a clearly visible label saying, “No food or drinks” [Page 16].

cases.question: Who counts as a laboratory buddy, and do friends reachable only by phone count?
cases.answer: A buddy is a fellow lab user who is working close enough to notice if you are in any distress [Page 16]. Friends on cell phones, in offices, or in hostels do not count as a buddy [Page 16].

cases.question: What does the housekeeping guidance say about spills and hallways?
cases.answer:
* Spills must be attended to immediately and thoroughly [Page 17].
* Hallways and stairways should not be used as storage areas [Page 17].
* Workbenches and shelves should not be overloaded with unused equipment, chemicals, or other materials [Page 17].

cases.question: Why must long hair and loose clothing be confined in a laboratory?
cases.answer: Long hair and loose clothing must be confined in the laboratory to prevent them from catching fire [Page 17].

cases.question: What is the difference between safety glasses and chemical splash goggles?
cases.answer: Safety glasses are for mechanical hazards, chemical splash goggles are for liquid hazards, and face shields offer extra safety when handling bigger hazards [Page 18].

cases.question: When does the manual recommend a face shield together with safety goggles?
cases.answer: A face shield with safety goggles offers maximum protection when working with large amounts of chemicals (e.g., 4-liter bottles) or in the vicinity of explosive or explosive hazards (e.g., vacuum systems with glass jars) [Page 18].

cases.question: What are thin nitrile gloves used for, and what thickness does Table 2 give?
cases.answer: Thin Nitrile Gloves are used for laboratory work, medical examinations, and <2 mil light-duty tasks [Page 20]. ThickNitrile Gloves are used for mechanics, chemical handling, and heavy-duty 2-4 mil tasks [Page 20].

cases.question: What use cases and thickness are listed for thick nitrile gloves?
cases.answer: ThickNitrile Gloves are used for mechanics, chemical handling, and heavy-duty 2-4 mil tasks [Page 20].

cases.question: How should broken glass be picked up and disposed of?
cases.answer:
* When dealing with broken glass, wear hand protection when picking up the pieces [Page 22].
* Use a broom to sweep small pieces into a dustpan [Page 22].
* Store glass pieces in a designated bin for broken glass [Page 22].

cases.question: Where must the laboratory keep hard copies of chemical MSDSs?
cases.answer: Hard copies of MSDSs of all the chemicals in the lab must be kept in a clearly labelled folder [Page 23]. This folder should be stored in a visible location, preferably near the door [Page 23].

cases.question: Should water be added to acid, or acid to water?
cases.answer: Never add water to acid. Always add acid to water. [Page 24]

cases.question: Summarize section 3.3 Fume Hood Usage.
cases.answer:
* Hoods use air-flow to reduce exposure to fumes, and users must check the anemometer for good air flow before use [Page 25].
* Obstructing air-flow is prohibited, meaning do not store chemicals or cover vents [Page 25].
* The sash of the hood should be kept as low as possible to prevent Vapor back-flow [Page 25].
* Chemicals must be placed at least 6 inches inside the face of the hood [Page 25].
* The user must remain outside the hood and never peer inside [Page 25].

cases.question: What is the maximum shelf height for large bottles and toxic, flammable, or corrosive liquids?
cases.answer: ● Large bottles and bottles containing toxic, flammable, or corrosive liquids should be stored on shelves below eye level (maximum 5 feet). [Page 26]

cases.question: How soon after opening should peroxide-forming materials such as diethyl ether be discarded?
cases.answer: Opened containers of materials that may form peroxides, such as diethyl ether, should be discarded within one year of opening [Page 26]. All such containers should be dated upon receipt and upon opening [Page 26].

cases.question: How often must lab in-charges bring accumulated waste to the collection point, and what waste will be accepted?
cases.answer: Lab in-charges are required to collect all waste once a month and bring it to the waste collection point [Page 27]. Only labelled and segregated waste will be collected [Page 27].

cases.question: What minimum walking space must be maintained for fire safety?
cases.answer: ● Maintain adequate walking space in the laboratory, minimum of 2 feet, and unobstructed access to exits. [Page 27]

cases.question: What example does the manual give of overloading an electrical outlet?
cases.answer: Overloading an electrical outlet can lead to fire in that circuit [Page 28]. For example, do not connect a 15A device to a 5A socket [Page 28].

cases.question: May water be used on an electrical fire?
cases.answer: No, you should not try to extinguish an electrical fire with water because it can result in electric shock if the burning wires are still alive [Page 28]. Use only the proper fire extinguisher for electrical fires [Page 28].

cases.question: Where must an oil bath be operated, and what solvents must be kept away from a heated bath?
cases.answer: An oil bath must always be housed in a chemical fume hood [Page 29]. Flammable or combustible solvents should not be used in a heated bath or placed near the bath [Page 29].

cases.question: In the fire-extinguisher table, what class covers metal fires and how should they be extinguished?
cases.answer: Class D. Metal — Magnesium, Aluminum, Sodium, Potassium, Zirconium, Titanium, etc. — D — Special metal extinguishers. Do not use ordinary extinguishers found in the building, or else a violent reaction may result. [Page 30]

cases.question: Which extinguisher methods are listed for Class B flammable-liquid fires?
cases.answer: For Flammable Liquids, Oils, solvents, grease, paint, etc., the listed methods to extinguish are B, Foam spray, ABC powder, and carbon dioxide [Page 30].

cases.question: What class and extinguisher types does Table 3 specify for electrical fires?
cases.answer: Electrical fires — Class E — Powder type; Carbon dioxide [Page 31]

cases.question: For a Class 3B laser, what energy range and procedural requirements appear in Table 4?
cases.answer: 3B — Required — Required — Suggested — 5-500 mW — serious injury from diffuse reflection to the eye or to the skin. [Page 33]

cases.question: According to Table 4, what energy and hazards characterize a Class 4 laser?
cases.answer: 4 — Required — 5-500mW — Suggested — > 500 mW — Hazard to the eye and skin from direct, specular, or diffuse reflection. Fire hazard. [Page 33]

cases.question: For the 0.99 mW Class 2 laser in Table 5, what are the flash-blindness and eye-hazard distances?
At what heights must a gas cylinder be chained to the wall?
cases.answer: Gas cylinders must be chained to the wall at either half height or two chains at 1/3 and 2/3 height [Page 38]. This ensures the cylinder stays vertical if the valve fails [Page 38].

cases.question: Who may issue the all-clear after evacuation, and may anyone re-enter before it is issued?
cases.answer: The emergency response team (ERT) is the only one who can issue an “all-clear” after an evacuation in consultation with the lab in charge [Page 44]. No one can enter the building until the ERT has issued the all-clear [Page 44].

cases.question: What is the maximum number of people permitted in each laboratory?
cases.answer: The document does not contain information about the maximum number of people permitted in each laboratory.

cases.question: What exact telephone number should I call for the IITH health centre?
cases.answer: The document does not contain the exact telephone number for the IITH health centre. It lists the numbers for the IITH health centre as one of the emergency contact numbers that should be posted near the phone [Page 16].
